scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original C1 assessment of institutional support and learners' agency; awaiting independent pedagogical approval.

questions.q: What does the writer accept about a growth-oriented approach?
choices: It can empower learners while still masking structural obstacles.
It is effective only when students have equal resources.
It makes traditional grades irrelevant to students.
It prevents all learners from experiencing failure.
questions.explanation: The introduction recognises the benefits of resilience while questioning its potential to conceal unequal conditions.

questions.q: Why is judging the two students by effort alone problematic?
choices: Their teacher may be using different assessment criteria.
Both learners necessarily need different methods.
Their identical marks prove that material resources are unimportant.
Their opportunities to turn effort into progress are unequal.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph distinguishes visible effort from the circumstances that can make it productive.

questions.q: What assumption is challenged by the examples of debates and hobbies?
choices: Leisure should be assessed in the same way as homework.
Every worthwhile learning experience must produce measurable progress.
Informal discussion is necessarily more valuable than formal education.
Students learn only when a disagreement reaches a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues for experiences whose value cannot readily be converted into a measured outcome.

questions.q: Why does the writer note that advice cannot create extra time?
choices: To imply that planning is never an effective study strategy.
To identify a practical limit on individual advice.
To suggest that timetables explain every difference in results.
To demonstrate that the first learner is less motivated.
questions.explanation: Time and quiet space are resources that encouragement alone cannot provide.

questions.q: What danger is conveyed by curiosity becoming 'another obligation'?
choices: Students may become unwilling to read novels.
Teachers may have to grade every hobby.
Voluntary exploration could become another demand for productivity.
Learners could forget to complete their assessed assignments.
questions.explanation: The writer warns that treating every activity as self-optimisation can undermine curiosity itself.

questions.q: How does the conclusion connect institutional responsibility with personal agency?
choices: It removes the need for students to make decisions.
It recommends identical study strategies for everyone.
It regards the school's intervention as more important than student choice.
It argues that support can make independent decisions more meaningful.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph proposes institutional resources without eliminating students' responsibility.

questions.q: A school praises a pupil who studies in a crowded home every night. What concern follows from the text?
choices: Praise might distract the school from improving an avoidable obstacle.
The pupil should be discouraged from further study.
The school should reward the pupil with a higher examination mark.
The pupil should be told not to ask for additional support.
questions.explanation: Celebrating endurance risks overlooking the inadequate conditions that require it.

questions.q: A school ranks after-school clubs by examination gains. What could be overlooked?
choices: The number of students attending each club.
The resources available to each school department.
Valuable exploration and discussion without measurable outcomes.
The ability to schedule more compulsory revision sessions.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three defends forms of learning that are difficult to quantify.

questions.q: Why are specific feedback and supervised study space complementary?
choices: They make every pupil choose the same approach.
They improve both guidance and opportunities to act on it.
They shift all responsibility for results onto school staff.
They eliminate differences in students' available time.
questions.explanation: The conclusion calls for both effective strategies and support that enables students to use them.

questions.q: Which practice would the author most likely challenge?
choices: Allowing learners to revise an argument after receiving feedback.
Offering access to a supervised study room.
Recognising that rest can support well-being.
Requiring measurable self-improvement during all leisure activities.
questions.explanation: The author objects to treating even leisure as an obligation to demonstrate constant improvement.
